title: Names of the Eucharist (CCC 1328–1332)
hook: Lord's Supper, breaking of bread, holy sacrifice, Holy Communion, Holy Mass

segments.voice: Yesterday, Confirmation's gifts: it deepens, strengthens and sends. Your line was sent. Did you say the true thing you'd usually keep to yourself? Day one thousand ninety-seven.

Evening, on the road to a village called Emmaus. Two disciples are walking out of Jerusalem, heartbroken, and a stranger falls in beside them. He asks what they're talking about, and then he explains the Scriptures to them all the way there. They beg him to stay for supper. At the table he takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them, and in that moment they recognize him, and he vanishes. That same hour they go back to Jerusalem to tell the others. Luke, in the Douay-Rheims, puts it this way: "they knew him in the breaking of bread." That phrase became one of the names for what Catholics celebrate at every Mass. And it's only one of the names.
screen: `TWO DISCIPLES, A STRANGER.` → `BREAD BLESSED AND BROKEN.` → `THEY KNEW HIM.`

segments.voice: The Catechism says the riches of this sacrament are so great that one name can't hold them, and each name brings out something. Eucharist, first. The word means thanksgiving, and the Catechism ties it to the Greek words in the Gospel accounts of the Last Supper, where Jesus gives thanks, and to the Jewish blessings that praise God over bread and wine. Then the Lord's Supper, because it's tied to the meal Jesus ate with his disciples the night before he died, and because it looks ahead to the wedding feast of the Lamb at the end. Then the breaking of bread, the Emmaus name. In Acts it's what the first Christians kept doing; the Douay-Rheims says they persevered "in the communication of the breaking of bread, and in prayers." Then the memorial of the Lord's Passion and Resurrection. Then the Holy Sacrifice, because it makes present the one sacrifice of Christ. The Holy and Divine Liturgy, because the Church's whole liturgy finds its center here. The Most Blessed Sacrament, the name for the Eucharist kept in the tabernacle. Holy Communion, because through it people are united to Christ, and to each other in one body. And last, Holy Mass. The Catechism says the name comes from the end of the liturgy, from the Latin word for sending, missio, because the people are sent out to do God's will in their daily lives. So the familiar name, Mass, comes from the last line, the dismissal. Each name opens a different window on one thing: thanks, a supper, bread broken, a memorial, a sacrifice, communion, a sending.
screen: `EUCHARIST: THANKSGIVING.` · `THE SUPPER, THE BREAKING OF BREAD.` · `SACRIFICE, LITURGY, COMMUNION.` · `MASS: FROM THE SENDING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say each name slowly. Settle, and breathe. On each out-breath, one name, quietly or just in your mind. Eucharist. The Lord's Supper. The breaking of bread. The memorial. The Holy Sacrifice. The Divine Liturgy. The Blessed Sacrament. Holy Communion. Holy Mass. Then go back to whichever name caught you, and stay with it until the bell. Ask what that one name shows that the others don't. If you pray, you can rest there in thanks. The bell holds the time.
Names of the Eucharist. Thanksgiving, supper, breaking of bread, memorial, sacrifice, liturgy, sacrament, communion, Mass: many names, each opening a window on one gift. Today's word.
Your line: one gift, many names. Today, when you break bread or share any meal, remember the road to Emmaus, and the moment at the table when they knew him. Day one thousand ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics in the Latin rite usually say Mass for the celebration and Holy Communion for receiving; Eastern Catholics speak of the Divine Liturgy, and the reserved Eucharist is called the Blessed Sacrament.

original.note: Greek: thanksgiving; the Catechism ties the name to the giving of thanks at the Last Supper.

what a scholar hears: Catechism 1332: Mass, from missio, the sending forth of the faithful at the end of the liturgy.

notes: Confirm Challoner wording of Luke 24:35 and Acts 2:42.
The meaning of 'Eucharist' (thanksgiving) and the derivation of 'Mass' from missio are both given in CCC 1328 and 1332 themselves, so they stay under the claims rule.
The list of names follows CCC 1328–1332 but is selected (e.g. 'eucharistic assembly' and 'Holy Mysteries' left out for length). Confirm.
Emmaus retold from Luke 24:13–35; 'in the dark' is from 'the day is now far spent' (24:29) plus their same-hour return (24:33); Keeper may soften.
Original: εὐχαριστία; confirm accent and pronunciation.

Editor pass: Emmaus return now follows Luke 24:33 ('the same hour', no running or darkness, hook and fork); 'Divine Liturgy' explained as CCC 1330 does instead of an unsourced claim about Eastern usage.
Audit pass: hook no longer says the Emmaus disciples were walking 'home'; Luke 24:13 says only that they were going to Emmaus.
